tldr: On Oct 21, a paper on extracting materials data from literature with ML and LLMs appeared alongside NVIDIA's Kumo Relational, which claims to beat supervised ML on relational data with no training. A physics-constrained ML tutorial followed on Oct 23.
whats_new: A survey (Oct 28) maps security, privacy and robustness risks of distributed ML and federated learning across cloud-edge-IoT systems, with a focus on heterogeneity.
why_it_matters: Earlier items cut task-specific training or encode first-principles constraints; the survey covers what breaks when training is spread across heterogeneous devices. All four are research items, not shipped tooling.

beats.headline: ML applied to data extraction and relational prediction
beats.summary: Two Oct 21 items on reducing hand-built ML work.

beats.headline: Physics-constrained ML tutorial for hybrid modeling and control
Survey of trustworthiness in distributed ML across cloud-edge-IoT

open_questions: Is NVIDIA Kumo Relational's no-training claim reproduced on independent relational benchmarks?
Does the distributed-ML survey lead to released benchmarks or defenses for federated training threats?
take_for_builders: Before adopting Kumo Relational, rerun it against your own supervised baseline on your relational data; if you train across edge devices, use the survey's threat categories as a review checklist.
